findings.where: Nav and footer links: the MantaHostels home wordmark (p1), nav 'Destinations' (p3), and footer 'Privacy', 'Terms' and 'Report content' (p6, p7, p9)
findings.fault: These links look like they work, but none of them goes where its label says. The home wordmark and the Privacy, Terms and Report content links all just reload this page. 'Destinations' points to a #destinations section that this page doesn't have, so the click does nothing. The only links on the page that work are the current-page 'How we rank' links and the email address.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker who wants to go home or browse destinations after reading the method has no way forward. A visitor checking privacy or terms before trusting the site, or a hostel owner who wants to report content, clicks and lands back on the same page. On a page whose whole job is earning trust, links that go nowhere look broken or dishonest.

findings.fault: The page names a competitor and contrasts its review window with Manta's. PRODUCT.md rules this out: the durable claim 'names no competitor', social review density is ground Manta must 'never compete' on, and Hostelworld is a gatekeeper whose consent request (#78) is still open. The section also strays from what the h1 promises: Manta's own method.
findings.who_objects: The founder, because it breaks the positioning and puts the pending Hostelworld affiliate application at risk. Backpackers, too, because a page meant to state Manta's method openly ends by knocking a rival, which reads as marketing rather than disclosure and weakens the trust the page exists to build.

findings.where: Top of the page: the large lede, the smaller summary paragraph, the numbered list of three points, and the first sentence of 'Ranking method'
findings.fault: The same few claims come round three or four times before any detail arrives. The lede says the method is published, a second paragraph sums it up, the list sums it up again, and 'Ranking method' opens with the list's first line, 'No hostel can pay for a higher position', word for word. Two sizes of intro text sit one above the other, and neither reads clearly as the summary.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker on a phone scrolls past a full screen of repetition before reaching anything new, and may give up thinking the page is all slogan and no method.

findings.fault: The whole page is unbroken prose at body size. The claims that carry the trust ('no hostel can pay for a higher position', the 100/50/25% decay) get no more visual weight than the surrounding detail. Paragraphs run to 8–10 lines on desktop and 15 or more on a phone. Nothing on the page shows the brand: no illustration, no worked example, no score chip, so it reads like a terms page.
findings.who_objects: The founder, because the brand names 'sterile/corporate' as the enemy and 'effortless' as the first feeling. A backpacker skimming between bookings can't pick out the two or three facts that matter and leaves without them.

findings.fault: The page never explains the fixed word scale (≥9 Loved, ≥8 Great, ≥7 Solid, below that Mixed) or shows what a score looks like on a listing. Those are exactly what a visitor sees on every listing and would come here to understand.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker who clicked through from an '8.4 · Great' chip to find out what 'Great' means doesn't get an answer on the page that claims to state the method 'in full'.

findings.fault: The published method has no date or version, such as 'Method last changed …', and the footer has no copyright year. The only date on the page belongs to the Hostelworld citation.
findings.who_objects: A careful visitor or a hostel owner can't tell whether this is the method in force now, or notice when it changes. A trust page needs a date to be checkable (first-visit trust item 13).

findings.where: 'Hostelworld, for comparison' paragraph, and the second paragraph of 'Ranking method'
findings.fault: The opening sentence of the Hostelworld paragraph runs to about 70 words, with three nested conditions and a citation in parentheses. The weighted-count passage in 'Ranking method' is similarly hard to parse. These are long, technical sentences in what should be plain-language task text.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker reading in a second language, on a phone, mid-transit, loses the thread and doesn't take away the point.

findings.where: The three-point list under the intro, and the decay list in 'Scoring method'
findings.fault: Both lists are numbered, but neither is a sequence or a ranking. The first holds three independent rules. The second holds sample points on a curve, so '1. A stay from this month counts 100%' puts a list number right next to a percentage.
findings.who_objects: A reader may take the numbers as an order of importance or as steps. In the decay list the extra numerals get in the way of the figures that matter.

findings.fault: The footer wordmark looks exactly like the nav's home link and carries link colour on its 'Hostels' half, but it is static.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who reaches the bottom and taps the logo to go home, as most sites allow, gets nothing.

findings.where: End of the content, above the footer
findings.fault: The page ends on the Hostelworld comparison with no onward route, such as a link to browse destinations or hostels. A visitor who is now persuaded has nowhere to go but the nav, and its Destinations link is dead.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker who came here to check the ranking before choosing a hostel has to find their own way back to searching, and some won't.
